canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Sine and Cosine
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \sin x \, \textrm dx = -\cos x + C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =3\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Secant-Tangent and Cosecant-Cotangent
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \csc x \cot x \, \textrm dx = - \csc x + C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =-\int (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+C \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Secant Squared
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the integral $\displaystyle{\int} (2\sec^2 x + \sec x \tan x )\, \textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\int \sec^2 x \, \textrm dx = \tan x + C
$$

and

$$
\int \sec x \tan x \, \textrm dx = \sec x + C.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int (2\sec^2 x + \sec x \tan x )\, \textrm{d}x& = 2 \int \sec^2 x \, \textrm{d}x+ \int \sec x \tan x \, \textrm{d}x \
										&=2\tan x + \sec x + C.

}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating Cosecant Squared
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\int \csc^2 x \, \textrm dx = -\cot x + C
$$

and

$$
\int \csc x \cot x \, \textrm dx = -\csc x + C.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x(\operatorname{csc}⁡x+3\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x+3\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+3\int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-3\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We know that the derivative of sine is cosine:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sin{x}) = \cos{x}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we see that the integral of cosine is sine:

$$
\int \cos{x}\,\textrm d x = \sin{x} + C
$$

We can discover two other integrals by considering the derivatives of cosine and tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, by considering the derivatives of secant, cosecant, and cotangent, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C \\ \int {csc}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

With these six formulas, we can integrate many different trigonometric functions.
